results.mined_quantity: Pooled SMD (random effects) of an exercise-only intervention against a non-exercise control on global cognition in older adults with clinically diagnosed MCI, from RCTs, at the end of the intervention. Duration is an unresolved part of the estimand: 12 months or more (P-249) against 6-48 weeks (P-674).
results.quantity:
The two pooled figures estimate different quantities.

P-249 (Reparaz-Escudero 2024): pooled SMD (random effects, HKSJ) of LONG-TERM exercise alone, in programmes of 12 months or more, against a sham/stretching/social-activity control. Outcome is global cognition as change from baseline to end of study, which is 12 months for all three MCI trials. Population is community-dwelling older adults with MCI at baseline, k=3 (van Uffelen 2008, Lam 2012, Lam 2015): SMD 0.06 (95% CI -0.10 to 0.21).

P-674 (Ahn & Kim 2023): pooled SMD (DerSimonian-Laird, Hedges' g on change scores) of exercise alone against no treatment, usual activity, education, stretching, recreation or social activity. Outcome is global cognition at the END of 6-48 week programmes (18 of 21 trials ran 24 weeks or less). Population is adults aged 60+ with Petersen MCI in community, nursing-home and care-home settings, k=21: SMD 0.65 (0.39 to 0.91).

Only two P-674 trials reach 48 weeks (Lam 2012, Lam 2015), and both are also in P-249's MCI pool.
results.finding_a: P-249, p.12-13 (section 3.10): long-term exercise alone had "a negligible impact on participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline (SMD = 0.06; 95 %CI: -0.10, 0.21)". The trials are van Uffelen 2008 (walking, 12 months), Lam 2012 (tai chi, 12 months) and Lam 2015 (multicomponent physical arm, 12 months), per Table 2 on p.8. The per-trial SMDs in Fig. 3 (p.11) are van Uffelen -0.14 [-0.47; 0.19], Lam 2012 0.11 [-0.14; 0.36] and Lam 2015 0.11 [-0.13; 0.35]. The outcome is change from baseline to last follow-up (p.2-3). The overall exercise-alone estimate across non-demented adults is 0.05 (-0.04 to 0.13), k=9 (p.1, p.10).
results.finding_b:
P-674, p.3 (section 3.4): "The mean effect (SMD) was 0.65 (95% CI: 0.39 to 0.91)", from 21 RCTs (2,210 enrolled, 1,916 analysed), with I2 85% and tau2 0.2752. Outcome timing is "end of exercise therapy" (p.2), and Table 1 (p.4-5) gives durations of 6-48 weeks.

Fig. 3 (p.6) gives per-trial values. The two 48-week trials sit near zero: Lam 2012 0.16 [-0.10, 0.41] and Lam 2015 -0.04 [-0.28, 0.19]. The pooled 0.65 comes from shorter trials such as Bademli 2019 (20 weeks, nursing home) 2.69, Langoni 2019a (24 weeks) 1.45, Song 2016 (12 weeks) 1.35, Song & Yu 2019 (16 weeks) 1.16, Wei & Ji 2014 (24 weeks) 1.08, and Lam 2011 (coded 8 weeks) 1.01 [0.78, 1.25].

The sensitivity section (p.5) quotes "0.53 in all studies", which does not match 0.65.
results.same_quantity:
No. The element that fails is horizon and dose.

- Comparison: both are exercise alone against a non-exercise control, so the class broadly matches. The mix differs: all three of P-249's MCI trials used active or sham controls (sham activity, stretching, social activities), while most P-674 trials used usual activity or education.
- Outcome and metric: matched. Both pool global cognition as an SMD of change from baseline across mixed instruments. P-674's Fig. 3 shows within-group change means (e.g. Lam 2015 -0.2 vs -0.1; Bademli 3.27 vs -1.18), so the effect-size construction does not separate the two.
- Horizon and dose: NOT matched. P-249 requires programmes of at least 12 months and measures at 12 months or later. P-674 measures at the end of programmes of mostly 8-24 weeks; 18 of its 21 cognition trials ran 24 weeks or less, and only Lam 2012 and Lam 2015 reach 48 weeks. The rule's reading lists horizon as part of the same estimand.
- Population: both are older adults with clinically diagnosed MCI (Petersen, CDR 0.5 or IWG criteria), so the class matches. However, P-249 admits only community-dwelling adults, while P-674 includes nursing-home and care-home trials (Bademli, Varela, Wei & Ji); its facility subgroup gives SMD 1.43.
- Design: RCTs in both.

The two source documents show that horizon is the separating condition. At the horizon they share (the 48-week / 12-month Hong Kong trials), P-674 estimates 0.16 and -0.04 and P-249 estimates 0.11 and 0.11. P-674 also enters the same randomised Hong Kong cohort twice (R=171:218): at its interim point (Lam 2011, g=1.01) and at 1 year (Lam 2012, g=0.16). So inside P-674 itself, horizon changes the estimate for one trial.
results.incompatible:
No, not on any shared quantity. As printed, the two pooled intervals are disjoint (P-249's upper bound 0.21 is below P-674's lower bound 0.39), so they would be incompatible if they measured the same quantity. They do not. P-249 pools only interventions of 12 months or more; P-674's pooled value averages end-of-programme effects from mostly 8-24 week trials.

On the one quantity both documents estimate, long-duration exercise in MCI at about 12 months, they agree:
- P-674: Lam 2012 0.16 [-0.10, 0.41] and Lam 2015 -0.04 [-0.28, 0.19]
- P-249: Lam 2012 0.11 [-0.14, 0.36], Lam 2015 0.11 [-0.13, 0.35], and MCI pool 0.06 [-0.10, 0.21]

All of these intervals overlap. The gap between the pooled numbers comes from the short-duration trials that P-249 excludes by design. Other differences that go with duration remain untested: passive controls, small trials, facility settings, and the double entry of the Lam trial. The disagreement is between different estimands, not a contradiction about one.
results.gates:
- Task: matched (both T6 in the registry; syntheses of intervention trials).
- Dataset family: different trial pools that overlap on two trials (Lam 2012, Lam 2015). A waiver would have been available on population grounds ("population-level intervention effect; both older adults with clinically diagnosed MCI"), though P-249 is community-only and P-674 includes facility residents. The pair does not fail here; it fails the endpoint/horizon compatibility judged at adjudication.
- Validation tier: not applicable to syntheses, so counted as matched.
- Modality family: matched (global cognition measured by clinical screening instruments such as MMSE, MoCA, ADAS-Cog and CDR-SoB/NCSE, pooled as SMD). The registry's modality strings differ (P-249 "Behavioural/digital" vs P-674 cognitive scales), but the measurement class is the same.
- Endpoint and metric type: the metric matches (change-score SMD). The endpoint horizon does not: 12 months or more after programmes of at least 12 months, against the end of 6-48 week programmes. This is the failing element.
results.independence: These are distinct studies by unrelated author groups (Navarrabiomed/UPNA, Spain; Kangwon National University, Korea). Non-independence goes on the record: two of the three trials in P-249's MCI subgroup (Lam 2012, Lam 2015) are also in P-674's pool, and P-674 enters the Lam 2011/2012 Hong Kong trial twice.
results.manuscript_statement: Not applicable: the verdict is not genuine.

quotes.quote: The interventions consisted of long-term (≥12 months) physical exercise alone or in combination with other non-pharmacological strategies.
changes in global cognitive function, with the latter defined as the change in any validated measure of cognitive function from baseline to the last follow-up.
a negligible impact on participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline (SMD = 0.06; 95 %CI: −0.10, 0.21) (van Uffelen et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2012, 2015)

comparisons: no treatment, usual care, health education, and stretching; outcomes: the primary outcome was global cognitive function, and the secondary outcome was depression; timing of outcome measurement: end of exercise therapy; study design: only RCTs.

results.mined_quantity: Obesity at or before the MCI diagnosis vs non-obesity (P-1081: vs normal BMI) in clinical MCI, US EHR cohorts, confounder-adjusted hazard ratio for incident all-cause dementia (P-1081 5-year conversion; P-1151 10-year window). Exposure timing differs: contemporaneous BMI category vs obesity recorded before MCI.
results.quantity: The two papers estimate different quantities. P-1081: hazard ratio for 5-year conversion to ICD-coded all-cause dementia, for obese vs normal BMI category, where BMI was measured in the EHR at the time of MCI diagnosis (mean imputed for 2.43% with no BMI). The Cox model was trimmed by backward stepwise AIC selection and covers US veterans aged 50 or over with ICD-coded MCI. P-1151: hazard ratio for ICD-10 all-cause dementia within 10 years, for an obesity diagnosis made at least 5 years before the MCI diagnosis (ICD-10 codes plus BMI as a proxy) vs no such diagnosis 5 years before MCI. It uses 1:1 propensity-score matching in TriNetX US EHR adults aged 50 or over with MCI.
results.finding_a: P-1081 (Irwin et al. 2024, VA Corporate Data Warehouse; 59,782 veterans with MCI; 15,420 (25.8%) converted to all-cause dementia within 5 years). Table 3A (p8, real training set, backward stepwise Cox), BMI with Normal as the reference: Obese HR 0.75 (0.71-0.79); Overweight 0.87 (0.83-0.91); Underweight 0.87 (0.72-1.06); BMI overall p<0.001. The three synthetic-data models give the same values. The text (p5, p7) calls high BMI 'protective'. BMI was taken 'at the time of MCI diagnosis' (p3). The paper does not state its BMI category cut-offs in the main text. The cohort is 96-97% male, median age at MCI diagnosis 71.
results.finding_b: P-1151 (Anagnostakis et al. 2025, TriNetX US Collaborative Network; obesity cohort 4118 MCI+obesity vs 4118 matched controls, aged 50 or over; 1520 dementia events among the exposed, mean follow-up 2280 days). The overall figure appears only in the Figure 2 obesity panel (p7), confirmed on the rendered page: HR 1.05 (0.97 to 1.13); RD -0.12 (-3.73 to 3.49). The text (p4) says obesity was 'not significant across all sensitivity analyses (Figures 2 and S1), with the exception of males with obesity (HR 1.13, 95% CI: 1.01 to 1.26; RD 3.20, 95% CI: -2.37 to 8.78)'. The exposure is obesity 'diagnosed at least 5 years before the MCI diagnosis', compared with 'those without the diagnosis 5 years prior to the MCI diagnosis' (p2). The cohort is 45% male, mean age 68.5.
results.same_quantity:
No. The exposure and the reference group differ in definition, and these are the elements that decide what is estimated.
(1) Exposure timing. P-1081 uses the BMI category recorded at MCI diagnosis, i.e. current body mass in someone already cognitively impaired. P-1151 uses an obesity diagnosis made at least 5 years before MCI and says the lag was chosen on purpose, 'to avoid confounding effects of recent diagnoses' (p8). P-1081's own discussion (p7) explains its protective result through late-life BMI decline tracking cognitive decline ('decreased energy metabolism leading to decline in BMI and cognition'). That reverse-causation pathway is exactly what the P-1151 lag is built to remove, so the two designs are aimed at different causal questions.
(2) Ascertainment. P-1081 uses a measured BMI category. P-1151 uses ICD-10 obesity codes plus BMI as a proxy, with no race-specific cut-offs. Its PS-covariate list and Table 1 name the code family 'overweight and obesity' (the Table 1 row is N/A in the obesity cohort), so the exposure may include overweight codes; the exact codes are in Tables S1-S3, which are not in the PDF.
(3) Reference group. P-1081 compares against measured normal BMI, with overweight and underweight modelled separately. P-1151 compares against people who had no obesity diagnosis 5 years before MCI. That group mixes normal-weight and overweight people and possibly people who became obese in the 5 years before MCI; the paper does not say that controls had to be non-obese at MCI. Recombining P-1081's categories into obese vs non-obese gives roughly 0.82, which does not remove the timing and reference differences.
(4) Outcome: both are ICD-coded all-cause dementia, compatible. Horizon: 5-year truncated Cox vs a 10-year window. This is secondary under proportional hazards, but it matters because a reverse-causation effect is time-varying.
(5) Metric: both are hazard ratios, compatible.
(6) Adjustment. P-1081 is a stepwise prediction model: age, race, ethnicity, sex, cerebrovascular disease, stroke, MI, hypertension, diabetes, alcohol abuse, sleep apnoea; the authors warn of collider bias. P-1151 matches on T2D, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, ischaemic heart disease, CKD, sleep disorders, depression, medications and more. Both condition on metabolic mediators, so this is a secondary difference.
(7) Population class. Both are US EHR adults aged 50 or over with ICD-coded clinical MCI, but P-1081 is veterans (96% male) and P-1151 is a general insured population (45% male). That alone would count as a moderator, not a class difference.
The decisive failure is element (1), made worse by (2) and (3).
results.incompatible: On the numbers alone, the intervals exclude each other: P-1081 obese vs normal 0.75 (0.71-0.79), roughly 0.82 when recombined to obese vs non-obese, against P-1151 overall 1.05 (0.97-1.13). The male stratum goes in the opposite direction and is significant (1.13, 1.01-1.26), against P-1081's 0.75 in a 96% male cohort, though it is one of several sensitivity analyses. So if the two were the same quantity, the results could not both be true. They are not the same quantity, though. Present BMI at the time of MCI diagnosis and an obesity diagnosis made 5 or more years earlier are different exposures with different reference groups. A protective association with current BMI in prodromal disease, alongside a null association with long-standing obesity, is exactly what the reverse-causation account (the late-life 'obesity paradox') predicts. P-1081 itself proposes that account. The numeric disagreement is therefore not a contradiction on a shared estimand.
results.gates: Task: P-1081 is registered T2 (conversion prediction); P-1151 is registered T4. This is a mismatch, but the contested quantity is an association hazard ratio in both, so it could be waived for an association comparison. Dataset family: VA Corporate Data Warehouse vs TriNetX, different. A waiver would be available on population grounds: a population-level association, with both samples being US EHR adults aged 50 or over with ICD-coded clinical MCI, and the sex mix (96% vs 45% male) treated as a moderator. The pair fails on estimand before any waiver matters. Validation tier: not applicable to an association estimate, counted as matched (the registry lists V3 vs V2). Modality family: clinical EHR in both, matched. Endpoint: ICD-coded all-cause dementia in both, compatible. Metric type: HR in both, compatible. Failure point: same-quantity at adjudication, on exposure definition and timing plus the reference group.
results.independence: Distinct studies with no shared authors and distinct data sources (VA CDW 1999-2016 vs the TriNetX US Collaborative Network with 2010-2017 enrolment). Independent; no non-independence to record.

results.mined_quantity: Adjusted per-year association of baseline age with reversion from MCI to normal cognition in community-dwelling older adults with MCI (reversion vs non-reversion)
results.quantity: The two studies estimate different things. P-671 (Katayama 2021, NCGG-SGS, Obu, Japan): adjusted multinomial-logistic odds ratio per year of baseline age for NC status versus conversion (GCI, MMSE<24, and/or AD) at a single 4-year reassessment. Converters are the reference category. Community-dwelling adults aged 65 and over with psychometric MCI, and 325 of the 769 outcomes are imputed. P-986 (Overton 2023, GAS/SNAC, Skane, Sweden): adjusted Poisson incidence-rate ratio per year of age at the first MCI classification, for the rate per person-year of the first detected reversion. The comparison group is stable MCI only; dementia progressors and people who lost MCI eligibility are outside the 744. The offset is time to reversion or to the end of follow-up. The visit schedule depends on age: every 3 years over 78, every 6 years under 78. Ages run 59-94 and a cognitive complaint is required. The only estimand close to shared, reversion versus remaining MCI, is not reported by P-671. It can be derived as about 0.90 per year from imputed data, and even then it sits on a cumulative-odds scale, not a person-time rate scale.
results.finding_a: P-671, Table 5, p.6 (adjusted models): Age (years) OR 0.79 (0.75-0.84), P<0.01, in the reverters column; OR 0.88 (0.85-0.93), P<0.01, in the maintainers column. The table has only maintainer and reverter columns, so converters are the reference. Table 1, p.4 (the imputed group): mean baseline age 69.6 for reverters (n=256), 72.3 for maintainers (n=395) and 76.4 for converters (n=118); one-way ANOVA P<0.01, post hoc R<M,C and M<C. Of the 769, 325 had no second-wave cognitive examination and their status was estimated by multivariate normal imputation (p.2). In the 444 with observed outcomes, 232 (52.3%) reverted; after imputation the rate was 33.3% (p.4). If observed outcomes were kept, only about 24 of the 325 imputed outcomes are reversions (about 7%). The imputed statuses therefore follow first-wave covariates, which presumably include age. No age estimate from observed data only is reported. My derivation, not the paper's: reverters versus maintainers implies 0.79/0.88 = 0.90 per year, with an approximate 95% CI of 0.83-0.97 if the two estimates were independent. The paper reports no CI for this contrast.
results.finding_b: P-986, Table 4, p.12: Age (y) IRR 1.02 (1.01; 1.03), p<0.001, under the Petersen criteria (n=744: 323 reverters, 421 stable MCI). Under the NP criteria (n=375) it is 1.00 (0.98; 1.02), p=0.885. Model covariates (p.5): sex, age, education, cohabitation, physical activity, alcohol, BMI, cardiovascular disease, smoking, sleep disturbances, number of impaired domains and depression. The offset is time from the first MCI visit to reversion or to the end of follow-up, with a robust variance estimator. Average adjusted predictions (p.9): probability of reversion 0.38 at age 60 and 0.46 at age 70. Unadjusted, Table 1 (p.8): mean age at first MCI is 68.2 for reverters and 68.5 for stable MCI (Petersen), and 66.8 versus 69.3 (NP). So on the cumulative-proportion scale, P-986's own reverters are not older. The positive association appears only in the adjusted person-time rate model, and only under one of the two criteria. The authors call the finding contrary to most prior work and attribute it to selective attendance of healthy older adults (p.14). Visits are every 3 years over 78 and every 6 years under 78 (p.3).
results.same_quantity:
No. Element by element:
(1) Exposure. Chronological age per year in both. Matched.
(2) Comparison. P-671's reported estimate is reversion versus conversion to GCI/AD. P-986's is reversion versus stable MCI, with progressors excluded from the analytic sample. Age is expected to separate reverters from converters even when it does not separate reverters from people who stay at MCI. P-671's own maintainer-versus-converter OR (0.88) shows that most of the 0.79 is the conversion contrast. Not matched.
(3) Outcome and horizon. P-671: status at one reassessment after 4 years. P-986: the first reversion detected at any of several visits over a median of 7.0 years. The reversion definition also differs: P-986 requires a retained complaint and intact ADL; P-671 does not. Not matched.
(4) Metric type. Cumulative odds ratio versus incidence-rate ratio. For the age covariate specifically, P-986's person-time denominator depends on age by design, because the interval to the visit that detects a reversion is 3 years over 78 and 6 years under 78. Older participants also have more visits and so more chances to cross the threshold. Illustrative arithmetic, not in the paper: a doubling of the event rate above 78, fitted linearly over this age distribution (mean 68, SD 9), gives roughly 1.02 per year, the reported size. The paper gives no age-stratified or visit-interval-adjusted estimate, so the size of this artefact cannot be measured from the document. Not matched.
(5) Population. Both are community-dwelling older adults with psychometrically defined MCI (about 1.5 SD or below the 7th percentile, age-normed). P-671 is aged 65 and over and does not require a complaint. P-986 spans 59-94, includes 60-64-year-olds and requires a complaint. Broadly the same class, with a different age frame.
(6) Adjustment. P-671 adjusts for MMSE, walking speed and 4-year lifestyle-change class. P-986 adjusts for number of impaired domains, alcohol, cohabitation and BMI. Different sets.
(7) Data. P-671's estimate rests on 42% imputed outcomes; P-986's rests on observed attenders. The mismatches in (2) and (4) are each enough to make these different estimands.
results.incompatible: Not shown on a shared quantity. The two reported estimates, 0.79 (0.75-0.84) and 1.02 (1.01-1.03), do have opposite signs with CIs excluding 1. But they estimate different contrasts (versus converters against versus stable MCI) on different metrics (4-year cumulative odds against a person-time rate with an age-dependent visit schedule). Take the closest shared contrast, reversion versus remaining MCI. P-671's figure there is derived only (about 0.90, no reported CI, imputed outcomes). P-986's own descriptive data on the cumulative scale show reverters no older than stable MCI (68.2 v 68.5 Petersen; 66.8 v 69.3 NP). The opposite direction exists only in P-986's adjusted rate model, where the time denominator varies with age by design. It is also criteria-dependent within the same cohort: NP gives 1.00 (0.98-1.02). The authors themselves attribute it to a design feature. So the two papers do not report incompatible results on the same quantity.
results.gates: Task: T5 in both registry rows; matched. Dataset family: NCGG-SGS (Japan) versus GAS/SNAC (Sweden); mismatched. A waiver would be available on population grounds (a population-level association in community-dwelling older adults with psychometrically defined MCI), but it is not applied: the pair fails same-quantity on comparison and metric type, and the age frame differs (65+ versus 59-94). Validation tier: V2 in both rows, but not applicable to association studies; counted as matched. Modality family: the exposure is chronological age (demographic) and the outcome is classified from neuropsychological batteries in both; matched in class, although the registry modality_subtype labels differ (population_cohort_epidemiology versus neuropsychological_scores_only). Endpoint and metric-type compatibility at adjudication: fails (reversion-versus-conversion OR against reversion-versus-stable-MCI IRR with an age-dependent person-time offset).
results.independence: Independent. Different cohorts (NCGG-SGS, Obu, Japan; GAS/SNAC, Skane, Sweden), different countries and different author groups (Katayama/Shimada; Overton/Elmstahl). No shared authors. P-986 cites an earlier NCGG-SGS paper (Shimada 2019, ref 27) but not P-671.
results.manuscript_statement: Not applicable: the verdict is not genuine.
